title: Connect N Ropes with Minimum Cost
directAnswer: Connecting two ropes costs the sum of their lengths, and the merged rope is reused in later joins — so short ropes you merge early get re-added many times. The greedy fix is to always join the two SHORTEST ropes available. A min-heap gives you those two in O(log n): pop two, push their sum back, accumulate the sum into the total, repeat until one rope remains. O(n log n) time. This is exactly Huffman coding's merge step.

remember.pattern: Always merge the two smallest — min-heap, accumulate each merge cost
remember.formula:
heap = min-heap(all rope lengths)
total = 0
while heap has > 1 element:
    a = pop smallest
    b = pop smallest
    total += a + b
    push (a + b)
return total
rules: Each join costs the **sum of the two ropes joined**, and that sum becomes a new rope that participates in future joins.
Always combine the **two smallest** ropes currently available — a small rope joined early gets counted in every later merge, so you want small lengths to enter early and large lengths late.
A **min-heap** is the natural structure: it hands you the two smallest in O(log n) each and reinserts the merged rope in O(log n).
The total cost equals the sum of every intermediate merge — equivalently, each original rope's length times its depth in the merge tree.
This is structurally identical to Huffman encoding; the only difference is what the 'symbols' represent.
whenToUse: Repeatedly combine two elements into one, paying a cost equal to their combined size
The combined element is reused in later combinations (cost compounds with depth)
You want to minimise total combination cost over all merge orders
Building an optimal binary merge tree — Huffman / file-merge / k-way merge planning
antiSignals: Merge cost is constant regardless of sizes → order doesn't matter, no heap needed
You merge a fixed sequence in given order (no freedom to choose pairs) → it's a prefix-sum, not greedy
You combine more than two at a time with a different cost rule → generalised Huffman, tune the heap arity
You want to MAXIMISE cost → flip to a max-heap and merge the two largest
remember.takeaway: The cost of a rope compounds with how early you merge it, so the greedy 'two smallest first' keeps large values shallow in the merge tree. A min-heap turns the repeated 'find two smallest' into O(log n) per step. Recognise this and you've also solved Huffman coding and 'minimum cost to merge stones' (k=adjacent variant).

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you see that merged ropes are reused (so early merges compound) and reach for a min-heap to always combine the two smallest — rather than connecting in input order.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Connecting ropes in the given order or sorting once and merging left-to-right, both of which ignore that each merged rope re-enters the pool and must be re-considered against the originals.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain that total cost = sum over original ropes of length × depth in the merge tree, so you want small ropes deep and large ropes shallow — exactly what 'always merge the two smallest' achieves. Then name it as the Huffman merge.

problemStatement:
You are given an array `ropes` of `n` positive lengths. You connect ropes one pair at a time; connecting two ropes of lengths `a` and `b` produces a single rope of length `a + b` and costs `a + b`.

The newly formed rope can be connected with other ropes in later steps. You must connect all ropes into a **single** rope.

Return the ***minimum total cost*** to connect every rope into one.
constraints: Total cost can exceed a 32-bit int (up to ~10⁹·log n) → accumulate in a long
If there is only one rope, the cost is 0 (nothing to connect)
understanding: Think of building a binary tree where every original rope is a leaf and every internal node is a merge whose value is the sum of its two children. The cost of a merge is that node's value, and the total cost is the sum of all internal-node values. Equivalently, each leaf contributes its length once for every merge it sits under — its depth. Minimising total cost means keeping large lengths shallow, which 'merge the two smallest' does automatically.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does the merged rope get reused in later connections?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the crux. A rope formed early is part of the pool and gets added again in every subsequent merge it participates in, so its length compounds.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can I connect more than two ropes at once?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No, exactly two per step. (If you could merge k at a time, it generalises to a k-ary Huffman tree.)

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the total cost overflow 32 bits?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: With 10⁵ ropes of length 10⁴, sums accumulate well past int range. I keep the running total in a 64-bit long.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if there's only one rope, or none?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One rope or zero ropes need no connections, so the cost is 0. The loop simply doesn't run.

examples.explanation: Merge 2+3=5 (cost 5), then 4+5=9 (cost 9), then 6+9=15 (cost 15). Total 5+9+15 = 29. Always picking the two smallest is what gets here.
A single rope needs no connecting — cost 0.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: The decision tree to run before writing code. Reused merges + minimise total cost lands on the min-heap.

approaches.name: Repeated Two-Smallest Scan (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this to establish the greedy rule — always join the two smallest — before swapping the slow lookup for a heap.
hints: A merged rope is added again in every later join it takes part in. So a rope that enters early is paid for many times — which ropes do you want to enter the tree early?
Small ropes early, large ropes late. That means each step you should combine the two SMALLEST ropes currently in the pool.
Without a fancy structure: each round, scan the pool to find the two smallest, remove them, add their sum to the total, and push the sum back. Repeat until one rope remains.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each round scans the remaining pool (up to n entries) to find the two smallest → O(n) per round, and there are n−1 rounds → O(n²). The pool itself is O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Maintain a pool of rope lengths. Each round, find the two smallest ropes, remove them, add their sum to the running total, and insert that sum back into the pool as a new rope. Stop when a single rope remains.

**Why the two smallest, and why it matters that merges are reused.** When you merge ropes `a` and `b`, the new rope `a + b` doesn't disappear — it sits in the pool and will be added again in the next merge it joins, and again after that. So a length that enters the tree early is effectively multiplied by how many merges sit above it (its depth). To minimise the total, you want the *largest* original lengths to sit as high (shallow) as possible, which means feeding the *smallest* lengths in first. Combining the two smallest each step is precisely the rule that buries small values deep and keeps large values shallow.

**Reading the cost as a tree.** Picture each original rope as a leaf and each merge as an internal node valued at the sum of its children. The total cost is the sum of all internal-node values, which equals the sum over leaves of `length × depth`. 'Two smallest first' is the construction that minimises that weighted depth sum — the same objective Huffman coding optimises.

**Why we don't ship this.** Re-scanning the whole pool every round to find the two minimums is `O(n)` per round and `O(n²)` overall. We don't actually need the full pool sorted — we only ever need the two smallest, repeatedly. That's the textbook signal for a priority queue, which the optimal approach uses.
approaches.insight: The whole algorithm is one greedy rule — merge the two smallest — justified by the fact that merge cost compounds with depth. The O(n²) is purely the cost of finding those two minimums by scanning; a heap finds them in O(log n).

dryRun.intro: Each round scan for the two smallest, merge them, add to total, push the sum back.

code.python:
def connect_ropes(self, ropes: list[int]) -> int:
    pool = list(ropes)
    total = 0
    while len(pool) > 1:
        pool.sort()                 # O(n log n) per round on purpose: the slow baseline
        a = pool.pop(0)
        b = pool.pop(0)
        total += a + b
        pool.append(a + b)
    return total

java.explanation: Scan the pool for the smallest rope's index — O(n).
Second scan for the next smallest, skipping the first pick.
Remove the higher index first so removing the lower one doesn't shift it.

python.explanation: Sorting every round to expose the two smallest is what makes this baseline O(n²·log n) — the heap fixes it.
Merged rope re-enters the pool — this reuse is exactly why order matters.

edgeCases.behavior: Pool size 1 from the start → loop never runs → total 0.
Any pairing is symmetric; total is the same regardless of which equal ropes you pick.

pitfalls: Connecting ropes in input order — ignores that you can choose which pair to merge.
Sorting once and merging left-to-right without re-inserting the sum into the order — the merged rope must compete with the originals again.
Skipping this approach entirely — verbalising the 'two smallest' rule first is what the interviewer wants to hear.

approaches.name: Min-Heap Merge (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'I only ever need the two smallest, repeatedly — that's a min-heap'.
hints: You never need the whole pool sorted — just the two smallest, again and again, with one insertion after each removal. What structure gives min-removal and insertion in O(log n)?
Build a min-heap of all rope lengths. Pop the two smallest, add their sum to the total, and push the sum back as a new rope.
Repeat until the heap has one element. Heapify is O(n); each of the n−1 merges does O(log n) work → O(n log n) overall.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Building the heap is O(n). There are n−1 merges; each does two pops and one push, all O(log n) → O(n log n) total. The heap holds at most n elements → O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Put every rope length into a min-heap. While more than one rope remains, pop the two smallest, add their sum to the running total, and push the sum back. The final total is the minimum connection cost.

**Why a heap is the exact right structure.** The baseline showed the only operations we ever need are: remove the smallest, remove the next smallest, insert a new value. A min-heap does each of those in `O(log n)` — no need to keep the full pool sorted. Two pops plus one push per merge, over `n − 1` merges, is `O(n log n)`, with an `O(n)` heapify up front.

**Why 'two smallest' is provably optimal (exchange argument).** Consider the optimal merge tree. The two deepest leaves must be siblings (if not, you could move a shallower leaf deeper to fill a gap without increasing cost). Those two deepest leaves should be the two smallest lengths — if a larger length were deeper than a smaller one, swapping them would reduce `Σ length × depth`, contradicting optimality. So in any optimal tree the two smallest ropes are siblings at the bottom; merging them first and treating their sum as a single new leaf preserves optimality. Recursing on the smaller pool is exactly the heap algorithm.

**Why the total accumulates merge sums.** Each merge's cost is the value of the new internal node. Summing those over the whole tree double-counts each original length once per ancestor merge — i.e. `Σ length × depth`. Accumulating `a + b` on every pop-pop-push captures precisely that.

**Watch the overflow.** With up to `10⁵` ropes, the running total and the merged values can exceed 32 bits. Keep the heap values and the total in 64-bit (`long` in Java, Python ints are arbitrary precision).
approaches.insight: Whenever the baseline's bottleneck is 'repeatedly find the min (or two mins) and reinsert', a heap is the upgrade. Conceptually this builds an optimal binary merge tree bottom-up — the very same algorithm as Huffman coding, where ropes are symbol frequencies.

dryRun.intro: Min-heap = [2,3,4,6]. Pop two smallest, add sum to total, push sum back.

code.python:
import heapq

def connect_ropes(self, ropes: list[int]) -> int:
    heap = list(ropes)
    heapq.heapify(heap)
    total = 0
    while len(heap) > 1:
        a = heapq.heappop(heap)
        b = heapq.heappop(heap)
        total += a + b
        heapq.heappush(heap, a + b)
    return total

java.explanation: Java's PriorityQueue is a min-heap by default — exactly what we want.

pitfalls: Using a 32-bit int for the total — overflows on large inputs; use long.
Reaching for a max-heap by habit — this problem needs the SMALLEST two each step.
Forgetting to push the merged sum back — then the merged rope never participates again and the cost is wrong.

commonMistakes: Connecting ropes in the input order instead of always merging the two smallest.
Forgetting that each merged rope re-enters the pool and is paid for again in later merges.
Overflowing a 32-bit total on large inputs — accumulate in a 64-bit integer.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Sort once, merge left-to-right
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Sorting the original ropes and adding them in order ignores that a merged rope must be re-compared against the remaining originals. On [1,2,5,10] sort-and-add gives 1+2=3, 3+5=8, 8+10=18 by luck, but on [1,5,5,5] it diverges from the true optimum. You must re-insert each merge.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
ropes.sort()
total = ropes[0]
for r in ropes[1:]:
    total += total + r   # never re-sorts the merged value into place
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
heapq.heapify(ropes)
total = 0
while len(ropes) > 1:
    a = heapq.heappop(ropes)
    b = heapq.heappop(ropes)
    total += a + b
    heapq.heappush(ropes, a + b)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: 32-bit overflow on the total
commonMistakesDetailed.why: With 10⁵ ropes the merged sums and the accumulated total exceed 2³¹. An int total silently wraps to a negative number.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using a max-heap
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Merging the two LARGEST first keeps large values shallow but forces small values to compound — that maximises cost, the opposite of the goal.

patternNote: Canonical optimal-binary-merge-tree greedy, powered by a min-heap. Recognise it whenever you repeatedly combine two items into one at a cost equal to their combined size and the result is reused — minimise total cost by always merging the two smallest. Same algorithm as Huffman coding.
